What I Learned Rebuilding My Sourdough Starter Twice

Posted on September 14, 2026 by Noor

My first starter died in July, during the hottest week of the year, while I was away for a long weekend. The second one survived the heat but never rose properly, and it smelled like nail polish remover for most of August. The third one, which is bubbling on my counter as I write this, has been reliable for six weeks.

I made a lot of mistakes along the way, so I’m writing them down, partly for you and partly so that I stop repeating them. None of this is new advice, but it took me three tries to actually follow it.

1. Temperature matters more than flour

I spent weeks switching between rye, whole wheat, and bread flour, convinced that the flour was the problem. It wasn’t. My kitchen swung between 19°C at night and 31°C in the afternoon, and the yeast simply could not keep up with those changes. Moving the jar into a cupboard, away from the window, made more difference than any flour.

2. Feed by weight, not by volume

A cup of flour can weigh anywhere from 110 to 150 grams, depending on how you scoop it. Once I started using a cheap kitchen scale and feeding at a strict 1:1:1 ratio, the starter peaked at the same time every day, which made planning a bake much easier.

3. The acetone smell means it’s hungry

That nail polish smell is a sign the culture has run out of food, not a sign it’s dying. Feeding twice a day for a few days fixed it, and the smell turned back into something closer to yoghurt.

If you’re starting your own, my day-by-day starter guide has the exact schedule I used this time.
